items.title: Figure 15 caption question: Why does a magenta ball, which looks magenta in white light, appear blue under a blue stage light?

body.html: Magenta ball, lit only by blue light. Explain its color.
Magenta pigment absorbs green and reflects red and blue (color by subtraction).
The blue light contains only blue. The magenta pigment reflects blue, so the ball reflects the only light that is available and looks blue.

answer.html: The magenta ball reflects red and blue light and absorbs green. Under a blue light only blue is present, and the ball reflects it, so it appears blue.

check.html: A green ball (which absorbs blue) would look black under the same blue light.

items.title: Get It? (Color by subtraction): A stage crew mixes red and blue spotlights on a white screen and also mixes magenta and cyan paints on a palette. Distinguish color by addition from color by subtraction using these two examples.

body.html: Lights add; pigments subtract (absorb).
Overlapping red and blue spotlights add together to make magenta light. Magenta and cyan paints each absorb some colors of white light; mixing them leaves only what neither absorbs.

answer.html: Color by addition combines lights of different colors, so the colors add: red + blue light gives magenta. Color by subtraction happens when pigments absorb (subtract) wavelengths from white light and the rest is reflected: magenta paint absorbs green, cyan paint absorbs red, so the mixture reflects mainly blue.

check.html: The mixture of magenta and cyan pigments leaves blue, the one primary color of light that neither pigment absorbs.

items.title: Figure 17 caption question: Explain why autumn leaves appear in various shades of red, orange, and yellow.

body.html: Explain the variety of colors in fall foliage.
Leaves show the colors of the pigments that reflect light (color by subtraction).

In summer, chlorophyll absorbs red and blue and reflects green. In autumn the chlorophyll breaks down, and other pigments that were hidden show up: yellow and orange pigments absorb blue and reflect red and green, and red pigments formed in the leaf absorb green and blue and reflect red.

answer.html: As chlorophyll breaks down, the leaves' remaining pigments determine their color. Yellow and orange pigments reflect red and green light (absorbing blue), and red pigments reflect red light. Different trees, and even different leaves, contain different amounts of these pigments, producing the variety of shades.

check.html: Consistent with color by subtraction.

items.title: Get It? (Polarization): Draw a diagram showing nonpolarized light traveling straight toward you.

body.html: Light is a transverse wave; the electric field is perpendicular to the direction of travel.

answer.html: Seen head-on, nonpolarized light has its electric field oscillating in all directions perpendicular to the beam, drawn as double-headed arrows pointing every which way around the central beam direction.

check.html: Light is a transverse wave, so all oscillations are perpendicular to the travel direction.

items.title: Hubble question (Figure 23): The light from a star in our own galaxy shows spectral lines shifted toward shorter wavelengths than the laboratory values. What do you think caused the shift?

body.html: The Doppler effect changes the observed wavelength when the source and observer move relative to each other.
A shift to shorter wavelengths is a blue shift. By the Doppler effect, blue shift occurs when the source and observer are getting closer.

answer.html: The star is moving toward Earth (the Doppler effect), so its light is blue shifted. A uniform shift of all of its spectral lines by the same fraction shows this is motion, not a difference in composition.

check.html: The opposite case, a receding source, gives a red shift, as in Hubble's galaxies.

items.title: Check Your Progress 20 (Doppler effect): A student says that a star whose spectral lines are shifted toward the violet end of the spectrum must be hotter than a star whose lines are not shifted. Is the student correct? Explain what the shift means.

body.html: A uniform shift of all lines is a Doppler shift and depends on relative motion.

answer.html: The student is not correct. A shift toward shorter wavelengths (blue shift) means that the star and Earth are moving toward each other. A red shift would mean they are moving apart. The shift is determined by the relative velocity, 𝛥𝜆= ± (𝑣/ 𝑐)𝜆, not by temperature.

check.html: Matches the sign of 𝛥𝜆 in 𝛥𝜆= ± (𝑣/ 𝑐)𝜆.

items.title: Check Your Progress 21 (Addition of light colors): What color of light combined with red light gives white?

body.html: Red + green + blue light makes white, so the missing colors must supply the rest.
Red is already present, so the color that supplies green and blue together is needed: cyan (green + blue).

answer.html: Cyan (a mixture of green and blue light), the complement of red.

check.html: Red + green + blue = white, so red + cyan = white.

items.title: Check Your Progress 22 (Light and pigment): What color is a magenta T-shirt under (a) white light, (b) red and green light, (c) green light only?

body.html: Magenta pigment absorbs green and reflects red and blue.

(a) White light contains all colors; red and blue are reflected (green absorbed), which we see as magenta. (b) Of the red and green present, only red is reflected. (c) Only green light is present and it is absorbed, so almost nothing is reflected.

answer.html: (a) magenta; (b) red; (c) black (or very dark).

check.html: Same logic as the magenta ball under blue light.

items.title: Check Your Progress 23 (Pigment colors): What are the primary pigment colors, and why do they look the color they do?

body.html: Primary pigments each absorb one primary color of light and reflect the other two.
Yellow absorbs blue and reflects red + green; magenta absorbs green and reflects red + blue; cyan absorbs red and reflects green + blue.

answer.html: The primary pigments are yellow, magenta, and cyan. Each subtracts one primary color of light (blue, green, and red respectively) and reflects the other two, so the object appears the color formed by the two it reflects (yellow, magenta, cyan).

check.html: The primary pigments are the secondary colors of light, and vice versa.

items.title: Check Your Progress 24 (Combination of pigments): Which primary pigments should be mixed to make blue? Explain using color by subtraction.

body.html: Primary pigments: yellow (absorbs blue), magenta (absorbs green), cyan (absorbs red).
To get blue, red and green must be absorbed and blue reflected. Cyan absorbs red and magenta absorbs green, so only blue is left.

answer.html: Mix cyan and magenta pigments: cyan subtracts red, magenta subtracts green, and the blue that remains is reflected.

check.html: Yellow (absorbs blue) is not used, so blue survives.

items.title: Check Your Progress 25 (Polarization): Describe a simple experiment to tell whether a camera filter or a pair of fishing glasses is polarizing.

body.html: Malus's law, 𝐼= 𝐼<sub>1</sub>cos<sup>2</sup>𝜃: a polarizer's transmitted intensity depends on its orientation relative to polarized light.

answer.html: Hold the filter up to a phone or laptop LCD screen (which gives polarized light) and rotate it; if the screen brightens and dims as you rotate, the filter is polarizing. Or look at glare reflected from a shiny table through the filter and rotate it, watching for the glare to appear and disappear. A second check: hold the filter over a known polarizing filter and rotate; it should go dark at 90° and bright at 0°. (Sample answer; any reasonable test is acceptable.)

check.html: All of these use the cos<sup>2</sup>𝜃 dependence of intensity on the angle.

items.title: Check Your Progress 26 (Polarizing sunglasses): Light reflected from the vertical glass wall of a skyscraper is polarized parallel to the surface. In which direction should the axis of a pair of polarizing sunglasses point to reduce this glare?

body.html: Light reflected from a surface is polarized parallel to the surface. A filter blocks light polarized perpendicular to its axis.
The glass wall is vertical, so the reflected glare is polarized vertically. To absorb vertically polarized glare, the axis must be perpendicular to it, which is horizontal.

answer.html: The polarizing axis should be horizontal, so the vertically polarized glare is blocked while some other light still passes.

check.html: For a horizontal road or lake the glare is horizontally polarized and the axis is vertical; a vertical wall reverses this.

items.title: Check Your Progress 28 (Critical thinking): The light from a binary star shows a spectral line that alternately shifts to longer wavelengths and then to shorter wavelengths, repeating every 4.0 days. What does this tell astronomers about the star?

body.html: Red shift means moving away, blue shift means moving toward, so an alternating shift means the motion alternates.

answer.html: The star is moving alternately away from us (red shift) and toward us (blue shift) in a repeating pattern every 4.0 days. This is what happens when a star orbits a companion: during half of the orbit it moves toward us and during the other half away from us. The period of the shift is the star's orbital period, and the size of the shift gives its orbital speed. The orbit is caused by gravitational attraction between the two stars.

check.html: A steady shift in one direction would mean motion in a single direction; an alternating shift means orbital motion.

items.title: 3D Thinking (Evaluate Design Solutions): evaluate transparent solar-window coatings for office buildings (cost, safety, reliability, aesthetics) in a paragraph.

body.html: A design that turns glass windows into solar collectors by absorbing invisible light (ultraviolet and infrared) while letting visible light through. Evaluate four criteria.

answer.html: (Sample paragraph written here; student opinions will vary.) Transparent solar coatings absorb ultraviolet and infrared light and pass most visible light, so a window could produce electricity while still letting people see through it. Cost: the coating adds manufacturing expense per window, but it uses surfaces a building already has, so it could pay for itself over time. Safety: the coating works at ordinary temperatures and adds no moving parts, so the risk is low, though wiring in the window frames must meet electrical codes. Reliability: coatings may degrade in strong sunlight, and cleaning or weather could wear the layer, so long-term testing is needed. Aesthetics: windows would look slightly tinted, but this is better than bulky roof panels on a tall building. Overall, the design looks promising if its efficiency and durability can be shown to justify the cost. (No Internet search was done for this set.)

check.html: Addresses all four criteria asked for.

items.title: Figure 15 caption question: Why does the die that is yellow in white light appear red in red light?

body.html: Yellow pigment absorbs blue and reflects red and green.
Red light contains only red. The yellow pigment reflects red light, so the die reflects the only light available and looks red.

answer.html: The yellow die reflects red (and green) light and absorbs blue. Under red light only red is present, and the die reflects it, so it appears red.

check.html: A blue die (which absorbs red) would look black under red light, as in the figure.

items.title: Get It? (Color by subtraction): Distinguish color by subtraction from color by addition.

answer.html: Color by addition combines lights of different colors (red + green + blue gives white; red + green gives yellow), and the colors add together. Color by subtraction occurs when pigments or dyes absorb (subtract) certain wavelengths from white light and the rest are reflected (yellow pigment absorbs blue and reflects red and green).

check.html: Primary colors of light (R, G, B) are the secondary pigments, and vice versa.

items.title: Figure 17 caption question: Explain why the plants are various shades of green.

answer.html: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue and reflects green, so leaves look green. Different plants have different amounts and kinds of chlorophyll and other pigments, and leaves differ in thickness, age, and lighting (sun or shade), so they reflect different amounts of green light and other wavelengths, producing various shades of green.

check.html: Consistent with color by subtraction.

check.html: Light is a transverse wave, so all the oscillations are perpendicular to the travel direction.

check.html: 𝑣/ 𝑐= 0.023 ≪1, so the low-speed formula applies.

items.title: Check Your Progress 20 (Doppler effect): Describe the relative motions when light is red shifted and blue shifted.

answer.html: By the Doppler effect, light is red shifted (longer wavelength, lower frequency) when the source and observer are moving apart (away from each other), and blue shifted (shorter wavelength, higher frequency) when they are moving toward each other.

check.html: Matches the sign of 𝛥𝜆 in 𝛥𝜆= ± (𝑣/ 𝑐)𝜆.

items.title: Check Your Progress 21 (Addition of light colors): What color combined with blue gives white?

answer.html: Yellow (a mixture of red and green light), which is the complement of blue.

check.html: Red + green + blue = white, so yellow + blue = white.

items.title: Check Your Progress 22 (Light and pigment): Color of a yellow banana under (a) white light, (b) green and red light, (c) blue light.

body.html: Yellow pigment absorbs blue light and reflects red and green.

(a) White light has all colors; red and green are reflected (blue absorbed), which we see as yellow. (b) Green and red are both reflected, so it looks yellow. (c) Only blue light is present and it is absorbed, so almost nothing is reflected.

answer.html: (a) yellow; (b) yellow; (c) black (or very dark).

check.html: Same logic as the yellow die in Figure 15.

items.title: Check Your Progress 23 (Pigment colors): What are the secondary pigment colors, and why do they look that color?

answer.html: The secondary pigments are red, green, and blue. Each absorbs two of the primary colors of light and reflects only one: red absorbs green and blue and reflects red; green absorbs red and blue and reflects green; blue absorbs red and green and reflects blue. So the object appears the color of the one color it reflects.

check.html: Matches the text.

items.title: Check Your Progress 24 (Combination of pigments): Which primary pigments make red? Explain by subtraction.

body.html: Primary pigments: yellow (absorbs blue), magenta (absorbs green), cyan (absorbs red).
To get red, blue and green must be absorbed and red reflected. Yellow absorbs blue and magenta absorbs green, so only red is left.

answer.html: Mix yellow and magenta pigments: yellow subtracts blue, magenta subtracts green, and the red that remains is reflected.

check.html: Cyan (absorbs red) is not used, so red survives.

items.title: Check Your Progress 25 (Polarization): Describe a simple experiment to tell whether store sunglasses are polarizing.

answer.html: Hold one lens in front of a glare source (a shiny surface or a reflection from a window or road) and rotate it; if the glare brightens and dims, it is polarizing. Better, hold two pairs of glasses (or one lens over a second lens) and rotate one relative to the other; if the pair goes dark at 90° and light at 0°, the lenses are polarizing. Another way is to look at an LCD screen and rotate the glasses.

check.html: Based on Malus's law, 𝐼= 𝐼<sub>1</sub>cos<sup>2</sup>𝜃 varies with angle.

items.title: Check Your Progress 26 (Polarizing sunglasses): Using Figure 24, which direction should the sunglasses' axis be to reduce glare from the road?

body.html: Figure 24 shows light reflected from a horizontal surface; the reflected light's electric field oscillates parallel to the surface (double arrows along the surface), i.e., it is polarized horizontally. A filter blocks light polarized perpendicular to its axis.
To absorb horizontally polarized glare, the axis must be perpendicular to it, which is vertical.

answer.html: The polarizing axis should be vertical, so the horizontally polarized glare reflected from the road is blocked while some other light still passes.

check.html: Matches the text: reflected light is polarized parallel to the reflecting surface.

items.title: Check Your Progress 27 (Red light): Red light is slower in air and water than in a vacuum, and its frequency does not change in water. Does the wavelength change?

body.html: 𝑣= 𝜆𝑓 in any medium. The frequency is fixed by the source.
If 𝑣 decreases while 𝑓 is the same, then 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓 decreases.

answer.html: Yes. The wavelength becomes shorter in air or water than in a vacuum (by the same factor that the speed decreases).

check.html: Light bends toward the normal and crowds its wavefronts in a slower medium.

items.title: Check Your Progress 28 (Critical thinking): How do astronomers know the Milky Way is moving toward Andromeda, and why might it be?

answer.html: Astronomers measure the spectrum of Andromeda's light and compare the wavelengths of known spectral lines with laboratory values. The lines are shifted toward shorter wavelengths (blue shifted), which by the Doppler effect means the galaxies are moving toward each other. A likely reason is gravitation: the two galaxies, being relatively close and massive, attract each other, which overcomes the general expansion of the universe at that distance.

check.html: A blue shift means approach; gravity is the only long-range attractive force among galaxies.

items.title: 3D Thinking (Evaluate Design Solutions): evaluate STPV cells (cost, safety, reliability, aesthetics) in a paragraph.

answer.html: (Sample paragraph written here; student opinions will vary.) STPV ("hot solar") cells capture more of the Sun's energy by turning absorbed sunlight into heat and re-emitting it in wavelengths the silicon cell can use, giving up to twice the electrical energy of a basic PV cell. Cost: the carbon nanotube absorber, nanophotonic crystals, and concentrator add manufacturing expense, but fewer panels would be needed, so the cost per kilowatt-hour could be lower. Safety: temperatures near 1000°C require insulation and shielding, which raises risk for roof installations. Reliability: more parts and high temperatures could wear out sooner than simple panels, and the concentrator must track the Sun. Aesthetics: smaller panels would take less roof space, though concentrators may look bulkier. Overall, the design looks promising if its cost, durability, and safety are shown to be acceptable. (No Internet search was done for this set.)

check.html: Addresses all four criteria asked for.

items.title: Data Analysis Lab, Wrap-Up Problem 1 (Claim): Would you give the driver a ticket or accept his explanation (Doppler effect, red 645 nm, green 545 nm)?

body.html: 𝜆= 645 nm (red), 𝜆<sub>𝑜𝑏𝑠</sub>= 545 nm (green appearance). Find the speed needed.
Doppler shift 𝛥𝜆= −<sup>𝑣</sup> <sub>𝑐</sub>𝜆 for an approaching source (blue shift, toward the light).
This is about 1.7 × 10<sup>8</sup> km/h, or 15% of the speed of light.

answer.html: Issue the ticket. To see red light as green the car would have to travel at about 4.7 × 10<sup>7</sup> m/s, which is physically impossible for a car.

check.html: A car on a road goes about 30 m/s, so 𝑣/ 𝑐≈10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup>, a shift of only about 6 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> nm.

items.title: Wrap-Up Problem 2 (Evidence and reasoning): How would you explain your decision to the driver?

body.html: At 30 m/s (about 108 km/h), 𝛥𝜆= (30 / 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup>)(645 nm) = 6.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> nm.

answer.html: "The Doppler effect does change the color of light, but only by a factor of 𝑣/ 𝑐. To change red (645 nm) into green (545 nm) you would have needed to be moving at about 4.7 × 10<sup>7</sup> m/s, roughly 15% of the speed of light. At even highway speeds the shift is about 6 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> nm, far too small to see, so the light was still red and I am giving you the ticket."

check.html: The shift for a car is about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> times smaller than the 100 nm needed.
